nodes.summary: Consider the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour of the traitors. Condition IC1 holds after $T$ rounds when any two generals $i$ and $j$, neither of which is the commander or a traitor, decide the same value after $T$ rounds of this execution.
nodes.title: Agreement condition (IC1)

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite set of more than $3m$ generals, at most $m$ of whom are traitors, and let the commander $c \in G$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with the value $v$, with no superiors and with all the other generals as lieutenants. Then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants decide the same value, and if $c$ is loyal, every loyal lieutenant decides $v$.
nodes.title: The oral messages algorithm solves the Byzantine generals problem

nodes.summary: In the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour of the traitors, the decision of general $i$ after $T$ rounds is the value that the decision function of $P$ assigns to $i$ in its state after $T$ rounds.
nodes.title: Decision of a general

nodes.summary: Suppose there are at least two possible orders. For every oral-message protocol for three generals $0$, $1$, $2$ with commander $0$ and every number of rounds $T$, there are an order $v$, a general $t$ and a behaviour of $t$ such that, in the execution with order $v$ in which $t$ is the only traitor, the agreement condition (IC1) or the validity condition (IC2) fails after $T$ rounds.
nodes.title: No protocol for three generals tolerates one traitor

nodes.summary: In the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour $\mathrm{adv}$ of the traitors, the messages that general $i$ receives in round $r$ form the function of the sender $j$ whose value is $\mathrm{adv}(r, j, i)$ if $j$ is a traitor, and otherwise the message that $P$ has $j$ send to $i$ in round $r$ from the state of $j$ after $r$ rounds.
nodes.title: Messages received in a round

nodes.summary: If general $i$ is not the commander $c$, then the initial state of $i$ when $c$ has order $v$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to $i$ as a general other than the commander; in particular, it does not depend on $v$.
nodes.title: Initial state of a lieutenant

nodes.summary: When the commander $c$ has order $v$, the initial state of $c$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to a commander with order $v$.
nodes.title: Initial state of the commander

nodes.summary: When the commander $c$ has order $v$, the initial state of general $i$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to a commander with order $v$ if $i = c$, and the initial state that the protocol assigns to $i$ as a general other than the commander if $i \ne c$.
nodes.title: Initial state of a general

nodes.summary: If, for every value $x$, at most half of the elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the majority of $s$ is the default value (retreat).
nodes.title: Majority falls back to the default value

nodes.summary: If more than half of the elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the majority of $s$ is $x$.
nodes.title: A value filling more than half of a multiset is its majority

nodes.summary: The majority of a finite multiset $s$ of values is the value $x$ such that more than half of the elements of $s$ are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), if there is one (there is at most one), and a fixed default value (retreat) otherwise.
nodes.title: Majority of a multiset

nodes.title: No protocol for $n$ generals tolerates $m$ traitors when $3 \le n \le 3m$

nodes.summary: No protocol for three generals solves the Byzantine generals problem with one traitor. Suppose there are at least two possible orders. nodes.title: No protocol for three generals solves the Byzantine generals problem with one traitor

nodes.summary: Let a commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants with $c \notin S$. If there are more than $3m$ generals, that is $3m < |S| + 1$, and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants $p, p' \in S$ decide the same value.
nodes.title: Agreement under oral messages (IC1)

nodes.summary: Let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $2k + m < |S| + 1$ (more than $2k + m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $k$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.

nodes.title: Oral messages achieve interactive consistency

nodes.summary: Let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $3m < |S| + 1$ (more than $3m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.

nodes.title: A loyal commander sends its value

nodes.summary: Fix which generals are loyal and an adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a list of generals and a recipient. If the commander $c$ is a traitor, then for every value $v$, every list $\sigma$ of superiors of $c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.
nodes.title: A traitorous commander sends the adversary's value

nodes.summary: Fix a predicate saying which generals are loyal and an adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a finite sequence of generals and a recipient. The value that lieutenant $p$ receives from commander $c$, who holds the value $v$ and whose superiors form the sequence $\sigma$, is $v$ if $c$ is loyal, and is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$ if $c$ is a traitor, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
